newsitem.title: UK: British meat inspectors warn of abattoir risk.
newsitem.headline: British meat inspectors warn of abattoir risk.

text.p: The body representing inspectors of meat processed by British abattoirs warned of "a potential time bomb" because of falling standards of hygiene, documents made available to journalists on Tuesday showed.

The Association of Meat Inspectors has told the government faecal contamination of carcases, blamed for an outbreak of food poisoning in Scotland which killed 20 people, "appears to be becoming an acceptable infringement of regulations".
The warning was contained in a letter written in February to junior agriculture minister Angela Browning by the Association's general secretary Peter Comrie.

The opposition Labour Party, which last week accused the government of covering up a report on abattoir standards, published Comrie's letter along with two others to Johnston McNeil, chief executive of the Meat Hygiene Service.
In January, Comrie told McNeil: "It appears from the very many phone calls from members that far from improving, standards of hygiene are steadily decreasing."
"There is no need to tell you that this is a potential timebomb, and I would urge you to implement measures, as in the BSE (mad cow disease) crisis, in order to overcome this dangerous situation."
Comrie wrote to McNeil again recently saying inspectors were being "actively encouraged to ignore breaches of regulations and in some cases threatened if they try to take action".
"Overall the system does not seem to be working in favour of public protection," he said.
Labour claimed that the letters showed that a statement which Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg made to parliament last week on government action to improve slaughterhouse standards was valueless.
Deputy leader John Prescott told BBC radio: "This is an alarming picture, and one that's quite contrary to what ministers were assuring us last week."

Labour, strong favourites to win a British election expected on May 1, has pledged to set up a Food Standard Agency independent of the Agriculture Ministry to ensure consumer interests are not sacrificed to those of farmers.

Prime Minister John Major told parliament that while he shared Labour's desire for "independent advice" on food safety, he believed there was still a need for a minister to be in charge, and to be answerable to MPs.
And Browning said in a statement there was no complacency in government on the issue.

She said every abattoir in Britain had been inspected and told what it needs to do to improve practices, and the Meat Health Service had already dismissed three staff and disciplined 41 for failure to enforce the rules properly.

Hogg has already been under fire for his handling of the BSE crisis which has caused a global ban on British beef exports and has cost the government 3.5 billion pounds ($5.62 billion) in compensation to farmers and other expenses. ($1=.6228 Pound)
